cells.tense: You are holding what you chose to hold, and it is holding well.
cells.act: say what you see in them only if they ask
cells.ask: Next time someone's in the middle of something hard, don't reach for the fix. Stay beside them, and if they ask what you notice about them, say it plainly and stop there.
cells.core:
There's a steadiness in you that doesn't need to be tested to be trusted. Somewhere close to home, you've picked up something that asks a lot, and you carry it while staying aimed at what you chose — no crushing, no bracing, just weight meeting a steady grip.

The next turn of the same steadiness is being beside someone in trouble without taking their load onto your own back. Not fixing. Staying in contact, keeping your own side, and letting them hear what you notice about them only if they ask. That's connection that holds without merging — your grip stays yours. The same steadiness that carries the weight also knows how to keep its hands off someone else's.

cells.tense: You are already bracing against a weight that has not yet been set down in front of you.
cells.act: adjust the share until it is fair, then stop
cells.ask: Over one week, note what you took on and what someone else did. Shift one piece of the split so it's even, then stop counting for the rest of the week.
cells.core:
You can hold what has to be held. That's real. And at the far edge of it, the grip is closed on things that no longer need holding — a fixed plan, an outcome you already chose, a weight you're bracing on someone else's behalf. What was resilient strength has started to read as rigidity.

Getting back to even isn't more effort. It's looking at what you're actually carrying, naming what each piece costs, and putting one of them back in someone else's hands — then stopping. Not punishment, not scorekeeping. Just proportion. The strength is still yours; it just needs a target you actually chose, not one you gripped ahead of time. You'll know it's working when the week stops feeling like a thing you survive.

The cell must be specific about the re-share and the stop, in the same week, small enough to be seen.

cells.tense: You have been waiting at a door that closed a long time ago.
cells.act: put it down and leave your hands empty a while
cells.ask: Pick something you're still carrying out of duty or protest, set it down on purpose — not lost, not thrown — and let your hands rest open for a short while.
cells.core:
Holding has stopped feeling possible. Where you once carried things without breaking, now the pressure lands and something in you lets go instead of standing. This isn't weakness — it's a body that learned holding is dangerous, and it moved to protect you. The direction you had is behind you, and you're still at that door.

What pulls you forward isn't more grip. It's clearing. Something no longer serves you and you're carrying it out of habit, so set it down deliberately. Not thrown away in panic — laid down. One deliberate release, and a stretch where your hands aren't full. That stretch is where direction comes back.

The ask must not push effort or feeling into the starved place — it pulls from the release, which is the inner motion already running.

cells.tense: The direction you are steering by has been set without you noticing that you set it.
cells.act: pick the one you would be sorriest to lose
cells.ask: Of everything you're steering toward, name the one whose loss would sting most — to yourself, plainly, no plan — and turn toward it once today.
cells.core:
There is a strength here you don't count as yours. You hold things under pressure — a job, a person, a promise — and it doesn't register as anything, only as what was required. The same with letting go: sometimes it was strength, and you filed it under 'I got lucky' or 'it was fine anyway.'

Nothing to prove. Just take the wheel back into your own hands in one place. Look at what you're already pointed at, and name the one whose loss would sting most. Let yourself want it, plainly, to yourself — no plan, no announcement. Then turn toward it once. What you actually chose is what's already been holding you up.

The ask must be a single turn, not a plan, and must not overrule the person's own account of what they've been doing.

attempts.check: Unsupported: that the person is carrying more than they should right now, visibly — nothing in the record says which weight they hold or have dropped. A reader could reasonably say 'I'm not holding anything, I've let everything go'; the asks survive that, since each is one small act that teaches something even if the read is wrong. The sentence that serves me more than them would be any line about bearing burdens, so every core drops it and works in the present with what the grip or the grip-release would look like as an ordinary action.
